comments.text: My mother was overweight and always thought she had too much trouble breathing.  Doctors always told her to get more exercise to reduce weight, but her difficulty breathing pretty much prevented her from exercising.  Nearly thirty years later, Mom's longtime doctor retired, so she saw a more observant doctor.  He figured out that her breathing trouble was caused by congestive heart failure - her lungs contained a whole lot of fluid.  And her excess weight was just extreme water retention.  Going on diuretics fixed both of those, and over the course of 45 days reduced from 225 lbs to 130 lbs.  Her heart was hugely enlarged after decades of fighting against the fluid, so she soon got a pacemaker/defibrillator.  The defibrillator function saved her life at least 8 times.  The diuretics put pressure on her kidneys, which became another life-threatening problem.  She had a very poor quality of life for many decades because of misdiagnoses.  She has amazingly survived all that.  She has deteriorating heath now at 89, but is very lucky to still be alive.
comments.author: @netgnostic1627

comments.text: Over 20 years ago I was a first responder and EMT in training. Was not allowed to work on people outside of basic first aid without detect supervision . So mostly was the guy on the radio and moving bags and equipment. One night we responded for three vehicle accident on the highway. I’m running equipment and updating dispatch and doing triage. Male driver is DOA. There is a little girl who bruised and banged up, has a dislocated shoulder, and has a head wound that looks worse than it was (head bleeding always looks worse), but thankfully has no major injuries. One lady is trapped and we are waiting on fire department for jaws of life (ETA 20 - 35 minutes). EMT’s are putting on emergency tourniquet so she doesn’t bleed out, as she has massive gash in her leg with twisted metal stapling her to the seat. She did lose the leg. Also has glass shards embedded though-out her upper torso and arms. Not only are we fighting the clock but are in a Zone of Death area (nearest hospital over an hour away). Another male with broken bones and crush injuries as he had been ejected from his truck, cannot get him conscious, but otherwise stable, loaded and on root to hospital. Finale guy is sitting on the road side, no visible major injuries, responding, telling us that he is fine and to work on others. He is moved to low priority as others are in more critical conditions. When we finally get to him I notice that he has been holding his head and ask him to do some AROM test for me. He would always keep holding his head with one hand or the other. Head EMT gets him into C-collar clearly worried but trying not to show it. After we get the patient loaded, my supervisor starts explaining to me that we had just witnessed an internal decapitation and it was a miracle that he was alive and even bigger miracle that he wasn’t paralyzed. They still use that incident in EMT training in our area to highlight that sometimes the most stable looking person is the one in the most critical condition.

comments.text: In his famous book THE MAN WHO MISTOOK HIS WIFE FOR A HAT, Oliver Sacks described the story of a patient who woke up and found a "dead, cold, hairy leg" in his bed, assuming a nurse played a cruel prank by placing a severed cadaver limb next to him. He tried to throw the "alien" leg out of bed, but he fell onto the floor along with it and realized it was physically attached to his body. If I recall, Sacks referred to this condition as somatoparaphrenia or a severe parietal lobe disturbance causing a total loss of body ownership. Something similar actually happened to Sacks himself after a serious injury. He describes the experience in his book A LEG TO STAND ON.

I didn't ask for anything but for them to see if I had injured my sound or dislocated a rib, if there was anything wrong that could explain it and maybe give me a way to fix it. They assumed I was drug seeking. They had a social worker come to evaluate me before they even looked at my back. Once they finally realized that I was a responsible adult without any history of drug use or even a SINGLE ER visit in the prior 15 years, they finally examined my back. And lo and behold, my upper back and neck were essentially one giant muscle spasm. 

I walked out with a 4 day prescription for painkillers and muscle relaxants, and a referral to a spine surgeon who found I had a herniated disc at C3-C4, and all the muscle spasms I had been experiencing (this had been coming and going for months) were from guarding it.

My medicalert bracelet (Australia) has a QR code linked to my medical information, medications and my doctors information.

There is also a phone number for ER or paramedics to call and confirm my information. I renew it annually. 

In Australia, there are several companies that provide bracelets but also provide a service where they keep details of your medical details. 

We also have a government health record database called My Health where you provide your health information, and any doctor anywhere in the country can access it. You have control over what information is shared.

We also have very strict privacy laws.

For the “you should have come in sooner” my dad..
Last year, he thought he had a UTI. Then spends the weekend vomiting and we think it’s food poisoning. He starts feeling better for a bit before nose diving. Thought he was having a stroke, call 911, gets taken to the hospital. Some urine retention but mostly just a bad UTI and he’s old, which I guess can cause confusion and stuff in older people. In the hospital for less than 24hrs, he’s perfectly normal the entire time, etc. gets sent home with antibiotics, figure it’s done. 
A week goes by. He finally tells me he needs to go to the ER because he’s having really bad pain and he can’t pee. I don’t find out until we get to the ER that he hasn’t peed IN A WEEK. A WEEK. They had to do a cath, and they filled up like 3 1/2 of those jug things. He was in pain because it was causing fluid to back up into his kidney and that kidney either had shut down or was starting to shut down. 
Few days in the hospital with a cath and antibiotics, and months with a catheter. Still isn’t 100% but is prob about 98%. Better than I was expecting, considering he’s 78. But I was so mad when I learned he’d let it go for a week 😂 like sir, 24hrs should have concerned you.

I had an “ear infection” that continued to get worse after several days of increasingly strong antibiotics.
Went to the emergency room in severe pain. After being admitted, the hospitalist told me I’d be sent home with antibiotics. She never even looked at my ear. 
The emergency room doctor called to suggest maybe I had shingles in my ear but the hospitalist dismissed the suggestion (again, without looking at my ear, which was now horrifyingly swollen). A few hours later, my lips stopped working. Staff dismissed my obvious concerns. 
Later that night, the new nurse saw how crooked my smile had gotten and sent me down for an emergency CT scan. No stroke so they put me back in bed. 
The next morning the new hospitalist told me “don’t worry, we won’t send you home until you’re feeling better.”
I said, “Doc, my face worked yesterday.” At this point the entire left side of my face was paralyzed. 
He said, “yeah, but we have you on antibiotics now.”
I said “I’ve been on antibiotics for almost a week.”
He said, “yeah, but these are good IV antibiotics so let’s give them 48 hours.”
Finally, an Ear, Nose and Throat specialist showed up and diagnosed me in seconds with Ramsay Hunt Syndrome (shingles in my ear). 
He switched me to antivirals and an incredible daily dose of prednisone.
Had we followed the hospitalist’s advice to “give it 48 more hours,” I may not have ever regained the use of half my face. 

All glory to God, though, I am fully recovered a year later.

comments.text:
UK Paramedic here. Two interesting cases I've had that I feel relate to this video:

First is the case that I always call my "Gregory House Moment":

- Elderly gentleman called due to pain in his left leg. No clear cause. No history of trauma. No red flags for DVT etc. So asked him to describe again what he was doing when it started (thorough history is always vital) and he explained how we had just walked up the path to get in a taxi when he felt light headed and afterwards his leg started to hurt. Asked if he had any other symptoms at the same time? For example any chest pain (at this point I'm thinking more about the light headed sensation, rather than the leg pain) and he replies "maybe a little". Cue a 12 lead ECG (EKG for the Americans out there) and boom, massive "barn door" STEMI. IV Morphine, Aspirin and GTN given, blue light to PPCI and it turns out his LAD was almost completely blocked!! (Cath Lab Nurse actually brought out the clot in a dish to show us - really interesting).

Second is a patient who went to extremes as part of her drug seeking behaviour:

- Young woman in her early 20's calls with dislocated shoulder. Tells us she's dislocated it multiple times before and now it just pops out for the slightest thing (makes sense so far). Tells us that, on that particular occasion, she'd picked up a shopping bag and it had come out again (again, makes sense given the history she's given us). She tells us she already took Paracetamol and Ibuprofen which did nothing. OK, I can believe that. Take a full history and she's a known epileptic, but medicated for it and tells us it's well controlled. So IV access and morphine followed by a trip to ED for relocation and imaging. On the way to hospital, she suddenly goes quiet and then starts to have a seizure. I shout through to my crewmate to put the lights and siren on, since we're close to hospital at this point, draw up Diazapam and give her the standard bolus dose, obviously cautious that she's already had Morphine so is at risk of respiratory depression. However the back of an ambulance is not a safe place to have a violent tonic-colonic seizure and I can manage respiratory depression if I need to. Arrive at hospital and my crewmate runs in to let them know what's happening and that we didn't have time to give them a pre-alert. Next thing I know a Consultant is at the back door of the ambulance telling me not to give her any more diazapam because she's known to them and has previously gone into cardiac arrest as result of being given them by ED staff, since she also self-medicates with codeine and diazapam at home. Turns out she intentionally dislocates her shoulder AND to make the (fake) seizure more convincing she'll drink a litre of water and intentionally wet herself whilst faking the seizure!!

Thankfully these days we have immediate access to digital medical records, so instances like the latter are easier to spot. That said, if a patient has a dislocated shoulder, I am not going to withhold pain relief. Would be more cautious though.
